1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Be7.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Cunningham Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Be7.background: Named after Alexander Cunningham, a Scottish jurist and chess player who lived at The Hague. Howard Staunton published sample lines of it in his Chess Player's Handbook of 1847.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Be7 4.Bc4.strategy: The most popular reply: the bishop eyes f7 and clears f1 for the king, so the check on h4 does not force the king to e2 where it would hem in the bishop. White develops and prepares for the check in the same move.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Be7 4.Bc4 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4 and keeps the check in reserve instead of spending a tempo on it. White's centre pawn is the target, so White has to decide how to meet the knight's pressure, while Black keeps the bishop flexible.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Be7 4.Bc4 Nf6.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Cunningham Defence, McCormick Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Be7 4.Bc4 Nf6.background: In modern practice it is more common for Black to simply develop with this move than to give the check on h4 at once.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Be7 4.Bc4 Bh4+.strategy: Checks anyway: White loses the right to castle, but the king is safe enough on f1 and the bishop on h4 can be attacked by the knight on f3. Black has spent time for a lasting nuisance, which is why most players simply develop instead.
